title: Scaling vs entanglement in measurement-induced phase transition for non-integrable systems
authors: Paranjoy Chaki, Protyush Nandi, Subinay Dasgupta, Ujjwal Sen
abstract: We find that the measurement-induced phase transition generated by deterministic global measurements, previously observed in the integrable transverse-field Ising model (TFIM), persists in non-integrable variants of the same. To address this question, we consider the TFIM with longitudinal field and the axial next-nearest-neighbor Ising (ANNNI) model. We show that both the survival probability and the bipartite entanglement entropy consistently capture a transition between area-law and volume-law entangled phases for two distinct initial states: a product state with all spins polarized along the transverse direction and a Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state. Finite-size scaling reveals a pronounced initial state dependence: for the polarized product state, the transition point follows an inverse-square-root scaling with system size in both non-integrable models, consistent with the integrable TFIM, whereas for the GHZ initial state, it deviates from this scaling and approaches zero considerably more slowly in the non-integrable models than in the integrable TFIM. These results establish the robustness of measurement-induced transitions under deterministic measurements against integrability breaking while highlighting the crucial role of the initial state in governing their scaling behavior.
summary: This paper investigates Measurement-Induced Phase Transitions (MIPTs) in quantum spin models, extending the study from integrable to non-integrable systems. By analyzing both survival probability and entanglement entropy, the authors confirm the robustness of the transition. Crucially, they demonstrate that the initial entanglement of the system dictates the scaling behavior of the transition point with system size.
main_problem: The study investigates the persistence and scaling behavior of Measurement-Induced Phase Transitions (MIPTs) when moving from integrable to non-integrable quantum systems.
main_result: MIPTs persist in non-integrable variants of the TFIM, and the critical scaling of the transition point ($\tau_c$) is highly dependent on the initial quantum state, particularly when comparing product states to highly entangled GHZ states.
method: The analysis uses diagnostics like survival probability and bipartite entanglement entropy, employing finite-size scaling techniques to characterize the transition point $\tau_c$ across different system sizes.
model_or_system: The models studied include the Transverse-Field Ising Model (TFIM) with longitudinal field and the Axial Next-Nearest-Neighbor Ising (ANNNI) model. The dynamics are governed by deterministic global measurements applied repeatedly to the system state.
key_observables: Survival Probability ($R_n$), Bipartite Entanglement Entropy ($S$), and the critical measurement rate ($\tau_c$).
important_parameters: System size ($L$), initial state (product state vs. GHZ state), and the longitudinal field strength ($h_x$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that deterministic global measurements are performed, and that the survival probability and entanglement entropy are reliable diagnostics for the MIPT.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the decay of survival probability ($R_n$) and its derivative ($dH/d\tau$) for both TFIM and ANNNI models, showing characteristic transitions. Scaling analysis plots are used to extract the system size dependence of the critical point $\tau_c$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the persistence of MIPTs in non-integrable systems by comparing results to the integrable TFIM. It then analyzes the scaling of the transition point $\tau_c$ using two distinct initial states (product and GHZ) to highlight the crucial role of initial entanglement.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses non-equilibrium phase transitions in interacting quantum systems, which is a major area of modern condensed matter theory. The comparison between integrable and non-integrable dynamics provides concrete insights into how system symmetries affect quantum criticality under measurement.
